newsitem.title: UK: Threat of mental illness rising, report says.
newsitem.headline: Threat of mental illness rising, report says.

text.p: A British journal said on Thursday that fewer research funds should be spent on infectious diseases and more on mental illness as this would be the developing world's most debilitating ailment by the year 2020.

The New Scientist, referring to a report by the World Health Organisation (WHO) to be released next week, said mental illness would be the next century's biggest killer, followed by road traffic accidents and coronary heart disease.
By 2020, traffic accidents will account for "one in every 20 lost years of healthy life worldwide", according to the report entitled Investing in Health Research and Development.
"These figures are a wake-up call," Dean Jamison, a professor of public health at the University of California at Los Angeles, told the magazine.
Jamison, chairman of the WHO committee set up to look into the best ways to spend research funds, found that relatively small investments could bring major improvements in public health.
"If we see serious changes in allocation of funds then we'll know that our analysis has made a difference."
Claude Romer, the WHO's head of safety promotion and injury control, called the report "a breakthrough in terms of reshaping the priority order of health issues".
The committee was critical of the amount of money spent on high-profile but less common diseases such as the Ebola virus, or attempts to improve vaccines that already existed.

The WHO committee used a new system to determine the toll from a particular disease. DALY, the disability-adjusted life year, measures loss of health as well as death and gives more importance to ailments that disable people.
"If you don't use a disability weighting you get into silliness because you pay no attention to, say, psychiatric illness or half the burden of road traffic accidents," Jamison said.
"Just using deaths by cause doesn't take notice of this."
The WHO report predicted that countries such as India, China, Ethiopia and Bangladesh could become the world's road accident hotspots.
